An aversion is a strong, deep feeling of dislike or disgust toward something — so strong that it makes you want to stay away from it, avoid it, or refuse to have anything to do with it.

It's not just a mild "I don't really like this." It's a powerful inner resistance. Think of it as your mind and body pulling back from something.
The Two Parts Hidden Inside the Word

Understanding aversion becomes easy when you see that it contains two ideas locked together:

  1. A feeling — strong dislike or disgust
  2. A behavior — the urge (or action) of turning away, avoiding, or refusing

These two parts almost always come together. When someone has an aversion to something, they don't just dislike it quietly — they move away from it, either physically or mentally. The feeling drives the avoidance.
How Strong Is an Aversion?

It sits on a scale:

Mild dislike → Dislike → Aversion → Deep repulsion → Hatred

An aversion is stronger than ordinary dislike, but it doesn't necessarily mean hatred. It often carries a sense of disgust, unease, or strong unwillingness rather than anger.

For example:

  • You might dislike doing dishes.
  • But you might have an aversion to eating raw onions — just the thought makes you feel uncomfortable and you actively avoid them.
What Can You Have an Aversion To?

Almost anything:

  • Foods — She has a strong aversion to the smell of fish.
  • Activities — He has an aversion to exercise and avoids the gym entirely.
  • Situations — She has an aversion to conflict and never argues, even when she should.
  • Concepts — He has a deep aversion to dishonesty.
  • People or groups — The child developed an aversion to crowded places after the incident.
An Aversion Can Be Rational or Irrational

This is important. An aversion doesn't have to make logical sense.

  • A rational aversion has a clear reason behind it. For example, developing an aversion to a certain food after it once made you very sick. That makes sense — your mind is protecting you.
  • An irrational aversion has no strong logical basis. For example, having an intense aversion to the color red, or to a harmless sound. There's no real danger, but the feeling of dislike and avoidance is still very real and powerful.

Both types are equally valid uses of the word.
Aversion Can Be Learned

One of the most fascinating things about aversion is that it is often learned through experience. If something caused you pain, embarrassment, fear, or sickness in the past, your mind can develop an aversion to it — almost automatically, to protect you from going through that again.

For example:

  • A child who got stung by a bee may develop an aversion to being outdoors near flowers.
  • A person who failed publicly while speaking may develop an aversion to public speaking.
Common Phrases and Fixed Expressions

These are standard ways the word is used that you'll encounter often:

"have an aversion to" — the most common pattern.

I have a strong aversion to loud noise.

"strong aversion" — the most common modifier. Since aversion already implies strength, adding "strong" is used for extra emphasis.

She has a strong aversion to being told what to do.

"deep aversion" — similar to strong, but stresses how ingrained or serious it is.

"develop an aversion" — means the feeling was not always there; it grew over time.

After the accident, he developed an aversion to driving.

"aversion to risk" (also: risk aversion) — widely used in finance and decision-making. Refers to someone's preference to avoid uncertainty or potential loss, even if it means missing a possible gain.

Her risk aversion meant she never invested in the stock market.

"aversion therapy" — a psychological treatment (used in medicine and therapy) where negative experiences are deliberately paired with a behavior someone wants to stop, to make them develop an aversion to it.

Aversion therapy was once used to help people quit smoking.
How Aversion Differs from Similar Words

WordWhat makes it different
DislikeSofter, more casual. You can dislike something and still tolerate it just fine.
AversionStronger, with a physical/emotional urge to avoid. Hard to tolerate.
PhobiaEven more intense than aversion — an overwhelming, often irrational fear that can cause panic. A phobia is usually clinical. An aversion is a strong dislike.
RepulsionVery similar to aversion but tends to be more physical and visceral — it's almost like your body recoils. Aversion is slightly broader.
HatredHatred usually involves intense negative emotion directed at a person or thing, often with bitterness or anger. Aversion is more about avoidance than anger.
A Few Vivid Examples to Make It Stick

• Despite being offered a raise, she turned it down — her aversion to office politics made corporate life unbearable for her.
  • His aversion to confrontation meant he would agree to almost anything just to avoid an argument.
  • The patient showed a complete aversion to the medication after experiencing severe side effects the first time.
  • Many people have a natural aversion to things that smell rotten — this is the body's way of warning us away from dangerous food.
The One-Sentence Summary

If you had to remember just one thing:

An aversion is a strong, often deep-seated feeling of dislike or disgust toward something that makes you want to avoid it — not just a passing preference, but a real, persistent pull away from that thing.
